## Encryption / Encoding (95)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AES Encrypt | redesigned | `aes:encrypt` | Bytes in and bytes out (CyberChef's Input and Output encodings are chain steps such as hex:decode and hex:encode). The key and the IV are key params in any of the key encodings, the key 16, 24 or 32 bytes. The mode is CBC (the default), CFB, OFB, CTR, GCM or ECB, and padding is its own choice (pkcs7, the default, or none), where CyberChef has separate CBC/NoPadding and ECB/NoPadding modes. GCM takes the additional data as the aad param and appends the 16-byte tag to the ciphertext, where CyberChef returns the tag separately. A wrong key or IV length is E_RANGE. CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. GCM needs an IV of at least 8 bytes (E_RANGE otherwise; CyberChef accepts any length, even none, which the library behind Forge does not). An empty IV is E_RANGE in CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR as in CyberChef. CyberChef's Include IV in output (Off, Prepend, Append) is a chain step: cat the IV in front of or behind the output. |
| AES Decrypt | redesigned | `aes:decrypt` | The inverse of aes:encrypt with the same parameters. For GCM the last 16 bytes of the input are the tag (CyberChef takes a separate GCM Tag param), and a tag that does not verify is E_COERCE and returns no plaintext; bad PKCS#7 padding is E_COERCE too. The no-padding modes of CyberChef are padding none. CyberChef's IV from input (From start or From end) is a chain step: slice the IV off the input and pass it as the iv param. CTR counts as in aes:encrypt (the last four bytes). |
| Blowfish Encrypt | redesigned | `blowfish:encrypt` | Key of 4 to 56 bytes (CyberChef's range), modes CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR and ECB, padding as a separate choice (pkcs7 or none). Big-endian words as in Schneier's paper. CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. |
| Blowfish Decrypt | redesigned | `blowfish:decrypt` | The inverse of blowfish:encrypt with the same parameters. |
| DES Encrypt | redesigned | `des:encrypt` | Bytes in and bytes out (CyberChef's Input and Output menus are chain steps such as hex:decode and hex:encode). Key and IV are key params in any key encoding; the key is 8 bytes. Modes CBC (default), CFB, OFB, CTR and ECB as in CyberChef, with the shared blockmode layer; padding is its own choice (pkcs7 or none). A wrong key or IV length is E_RANGE. CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. |
| DES Decrypt | redesigned | `des:decrypt` | The inverse of des:encrypt with the same parameters; bad PKCS#7 padding or ciphertext that is not whole 8-byte blocks is E_COERCE. |
| Triple DES Encrypt | redesigned | `triple-des:encrypt` | As DES with a 24-byte key, or a 16-byte key (two-key: K3 = K1, as CyberChef does); modes CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR and ECB; padding is its own choice. EDE form (SP 800-67). CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. |
| Triple DES Decrypt | redesigned | `triple-des:decrypt` | The inverse of triple-des:encrypt with the same parameters. |
| Fernet Encrypt | redesigned | `fernet:encrypt` | Fernet (github.com/fernet/spec) in FL over aes:encrypt, hmac:digest and base64: version 0x80, an 8-byte time, a 16-byte IV, AES-128-CBC with PKCS#7, HMAC-SHA256, url-safe base64 with padding. The input is bytes and the token is its text as bytes. The key is a key param: 32 bytes, or their url-safe base64 text (the form CyberChef takes; 43 or 44 characters), anything else E_RANGE. The IV comes from the host CSPRNG (the +random effect) and the time from the clock (+time), as in CyberChef, so the output differs on every call; nothing falls back to Math.random (a host with no crypto.getRandomValues is E_PRIMITIVE). Tests pin both through the private fernet:_seal. |
| Fernet Decrypt | redesigned | `fernet:decrypt` | The inverse, with the HMAC checked before anything is decrypted (E_COERCE for a bad token, a wrong key, bad base64, a bad version byte or bad padding). The key is the same key param as in fernet:encrypt. CyberChef fixes the TTL at 0 (no time check); an added ttl param (seconds, default 0 = no check) applies the spec's age rules: older than the TTL, or more than 60 seconds in the future, is E_COERCE. The base64 padding is optional on input. |
| LS47 Encrypt | covered | `classical:ls47-encrypt` |  |
| LS47 Decrypt | covered | `classical:ls47-decrypt` |  |
| RC2 Encrypt | redesigned | `rc2:encrypt` | RFC 2268. CyberChef runs CBC when an IV is given and ECB when it is blank, with no other setting; here mode (CBC, the default, or ECB) is explicit, so a blank IV in CBC is E_RANGE. The RFC's effective key bits are the effective-bits param (1 to 1024), whose default 128 is what CyberChef's library uses for any key length. Key 1 to 128 bytes; padding is its own choice. Effective bits that are not a multiple of 8 follow RFC 2268 (the vectors cover 63 and 129); the library behind CyberChef masks those wrongly, but CyberChef never sets them. |
| RC2 Decrypt | redesigned | `rc2:decrypt` | The inverse of rc2:encrypt with the same parameters, including effective-bits. |
| RC4 | redesigned | `rc4:crypt` | Bytes in and bytes out (CyberChef's Input and Output formats are chain steps such as hex:decode and hex:encode). The passphrase is a key param in any key encoding, used as the raw RC4 key of 1 to 256 bytes. The same word encrypts and decrypts. |
| RC4 Drop | redesigned | `rc4:crypt` | The same word as RC4 with the drop param, counted in bytes where CyberChef counts dwords: CyberChef's default of 192 dwords is drop 768. One word covers both rows because RC4-drop is RC4 with the first n key stream bytes discarded. |
| ChaCha | redesigned | `chacha:encrypt` | One word, encrypt, for both directions (a stream cipher), with the key and the nonce as key params in any of the four encodings (the Integer nonce toggle is not offered), the block counter as a number from 0, and rounds as a choice of 20, 12 or 8. The layouts follow noble: a 12-byte nonce with a 4-byte counter (RFC 8439) takes a 32-byte key and 20, 12 or 8 rounds; an 8-byte nonce with an 8-byte counter takes a 16- or 32-byte key and 20 rounds only. A 16-byte key with a 12-byte nonce, which CyberChef accepts, is E_RANGE, because noble has no such core and none is written here. A counter that would overflow is E_RANGE (noble refuses it), where CyberChef truncates. Input and output are bytes (chain hex:decode and hex:encode for text). The counter is limited to 32 bits for both layouts (noble's counter; the 8-byte nonce layout has a 64-bit counter in CyberChef): a counter or a message that would take it past 2^32 - 1 is E_RANGE. Rounds 12 and 8 are available for the 12-byte nonce only. For every combination that is offered the key stream equals CyberChef's. |
| Salsa20 | redesigned | `salsa20:encrypt` | One word, encrypt, for both directions, with the key (16 or 32 bytes), the 8-byte nonce and the block counter as CyberChef has them, except that the counter is limited to 32 bits (noble's), so one that would pass 2^32 - 1 is E_RANGE where CyberChef has a 64-bit counter. There is no rounds parameter: noble runs Salsa20/20 only, so CyberChef's 12 and 8 rounds are not offered (no own core is written for them). The Integer nonce toggle is not offered. A counter that would overflow is E_RANGE. |
| XSalsa20 | redesigned | `xsalsa20:encrypt` | One word, encrypt, for both directions, with the 24-byte nonce and the block counter as CyberChef has them, except that the counter is limited to 32 bits (noble's), so one that would pass 2^32 - 1 is E_RANGE where CyberChef has a 64-bit counter. The key is 32 bytes only: noble has no 16-byte XSalsa20, so CyberChef's 16-byte key is E_RANGE. There is no rounds parameter (20 rounds only, as for Salsa20), and no Integer nonce toggle (an 8-byte integer nonce is not a valid XSalsa20 nonce). |
| Rabbit | redesigned | `rabbit:crypt` | Bytes in and bytes out (the Raw and Hex input and output choices are chain steps). Key 16 bytes, IV empty or 8 bytes, endianness Big (RFC 4503) or Little (Crypto++), with CyberChef's key stream cut for a short last block. A wrong key or IV length is E_RANGE. |
| SM4 Encrypt | redesigned | `sm4:encrypt` | GB/T 32907-2016, 16-byte key and IV, modes CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR and ECB. CyberChef's CBC/NoPadding and ECB/NoPadding modes are padding none. CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. An empty input encrypts to one block of padding in CBC and ECB where CyberChef returns nothing. |
| SM4 Decrypt | redesigned | `sm4:decrypt` | The inverse of sm4:encrypt with the same parameters. |
| RC6 Encrypt | redesigned | `rc6:encrypt` | RC6-w/r with CyberChef's parameters: word-size (a multiple of 8, 8 to 256, default 32) and rounds (1 to 255, default 20); an empty IV is zero bytes as in CyberChef; modes CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR and ECB. Padding is pkcs7 or none: CyberChef's ZERO, RANDOM and BIT paddings are not offered (the shared padding is PKCS#7), and empty input encrypts to one padding block where CyberChef returns nothing. Word sizes other than 32 use BigInt arithmetic and are slow. CTR reads the counter block as a little-endian integer (the first byte is the least significant) and adds one per block, as CyberChef's RC6 does, so it differs from the big-endian counter of the other ciphers after the first block. The block is w / 2 bytes, so word-size 8 has 4-byte blocks (the modes work for any block size). |
| RC6 Decrypt | redesigned | `rc6:decrypt` | The inverse of rc6:encrypt with the same parameters. |
| Ascon Encrypt | redesigned | `ascon:encrypt` | Ascon-AEAD128 of NIST SP 800-232. The input is the plaintext bytes; the 16-byte key and 16-byte nonce are key params (E_RANGE otherwise) and the associated data a key param, empty by default. The output is the ciphertext followed by the 16-byte tag, as CyberChef. CyberChef's Input and Output menus (Raw or Hex) are chain steps (hex:decode, hex:encode). |
| Ascon Decrypt | redesigned | `ascon:decrypt` | Ascon-AEAD128 decryption: the input is the ciphertext followed by the tag, with the key, nonce and associated data of ascon:encrypt. A tag that does not verify, or an input shorter than 16 bytes, is E_COERCE and returns no plaintext. The Input and Output menus are chain steps. |

An empty input encrypts to one block of padding where CyberChef returns nothing. PRESENT-128 (the 16-byte key) matches CyberChef's. |
| PRESENT Decrypt | redesigned | `present:decrypt` | The inverse of present:encrypt with the same params. |

| GOST Encrypt | redesigned | `gost28147:encrypt` | GOST 28147-89 only, in the new gost28147 vocabulary (the existing gost vocabulary is the hash). | Derive PBKDF2 key | redesigned | `pbkdf2:derive` | The passphrase is the input (CyberChef's Passphrase encodings are chain steps). The key size is in bytes (default 16), where CyberChef counts bits (default 128). Iterations default 1 and the hash defaults to sha1, the choices sha1, sha256, sha384, sha512 and md5, as in CyberChef. The salt is a key param (hex, utf8, latin1 or base64), empty by default; CyberChef generates a random salt for an empty one, but a recipe must be deterministic, so an empty salt stays empty. Output is raw key bytes (chain hex:encode). Limits (E_RANGE): key 1 to 1024 bytes, and iterations times the number of hash blocks of the key at most 2,000,000, about 1.2 s for SHA-1 and 4.7 s for SHA-512, inside the 10 s bake deadline. |
| Derive EVP key | redesigned | `evp:derive` | OpenSSL's EVP_BytesToKey, written in FL over the md5, sha1 and sha2 digest words. The passphrase is the input. The key size is in bytes (default 16), where CyberChef counts bits (128); iterations default 1, the hash sha1, with the choices sha1, sha256, sha384, sha512 and md5, and the salt is a key param, as in CyberChef. CyberChef generates a random salt for an empty one; an empty salt stays empty here. A key and an IV come from one call: ask for both sizes and slice. Output is raw bytes (chain hex:encode). Size 1 to 1024 bytes; iterations cost about 18 VM steps each, so the untrusted bake step limit allows about 270,000 for one block. |
| Derive HKDF key | redesigned | `hkdf:derive` | Written in FL over hmac:digest (RFC 5869). The input is the keying material. Salt and info are key params (hex, base64, utf8 or latin1; CyberChef also offers Decimal, a chain step here). The hash defaults to sha256 and offers every CyberChef choice except Whirlpool-0 and Whirlpool-T, which Forge does not implement; the extract mode (with salt, no salt, skip) and L in bytes (default 16) are CyberChef's, and L beyond 255 times the hash length is E_RANGE. Output is raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| Bcrypt | redesigned | `bcrypt:hash`, `bcrypt:hash-salted` | The password is the input. bcrypt:hash draws a fresh random salt like CyberChef (its rounds parameter is the cost here, default 10, 4 to 16, E_RANGE otherwise) and carries the +random effect; the version prefix (2b by default, as CyberChef's bcryptjs writes, or 2a or 2y) is a parameter. bcrypt:hash-salted takes the 16-byte salt as a key param and is deterministic, which CyberChef cannot do. The output is the 60-character string as ASCII bytes. Only the first 72 bytes of the password count. The cost is capped at 16 (about 3.8 s) to stay inside the 10 s bake deadline; CyberChef allows up to 31. |
| Scrypt | covered | `scrypt:derive` | The input is the password. Salt is a key param (hex, base64, utf8 or latin1), N (default 16384), r (8), p (1) and the key length (64 bytes) are CyberChef's. Output is raw key bytes (chain hex:encode). Limits (E_RANGE): N a power of two up to 2^20, memory 128 * N * r at most 256 MiB, N * r * p at most 2^23 (about 2 s), key 1 to 4096 bytes; the defaults take about 35 ms. |
| JWT Sign | redesigned | `jwt:sign` | RFC 7519 over RFC 7515, in FL over hmac:digest. Only the HMAC algorithms HS256, HS384 and HS512 are offered; CyberChef's RS, ES and PS algorithms are public-key and belong to wave 7, and None (an unsigned token) is deliberately not offered. The key is a key param (not empty, else E_RANGE). The input is the payload JSON text and is signed exactly as given (it is not parsed or re-serialised, because FL has no JSON parser; it must be a JSON object by its first and last character, else E_COERCE). The header is {"alg":...,"typ":"JWT"} followed by the members of the header param (a JSON object text; typ there replaces the default, alg there is E_RANGE), where CyberChef merges a parsed object. CyberChef's library (jsonwebtoken) parses the payload, adds an iat (issued at) claim when there is none and signs the re-serialised JSON; here the text is signed exactly as given and nothing is added, so a payload that already holds an iat and is compact JSON signs to the same token. |
| JWT Verify | redesigned | `jwt:verify` | Verifies HS256, HS384 and HS512 under the key and returns the payload as the JSON text the token holds, as CyberChef returns the payload (a failure raises E_COERCE, there is no bool). The alg param is auto (the token's own header chooses among the three HMAC algorithms, which is safe because only a shared secret is accepted) or a pinned algorithm. alg none is never accepted, whatever the key or pin (E_RANGE), and neither is any algorithm that is not HS256/384/512 (RS, ES and PS are wave 7: E_RANGE). A header with the text "alg" twice is ambiguous (E_COERCE). Unlike CyberChef (jsonwebtoken) the exp and nbf claims are not checked: this is a signature check, because that needs a JSON parser and a clock. |
| JWT Decode | redesigned | `jwt:decode` | Splits a compact token and decodes the payload (or, with the part param, the header), without a key, as the JSON text the token holds, exactly as written (CyberChef returns the parsed payload). Each decoded part must be a JSON object by its first and last character, and the token three parts (an encrypted five-part JWT is E_COERCE); the JSON is not parsed further because FL has no JSON parser. |
| Citrix CTX1 Encode | covered | `classical:ctx1-encode` |  |
| Citrix CTX1 Decode | covered | `classical:ctx1-decode` |  |
| AES Key Wrap | redesigned | `aes-kw:wrap` | RFC 3394 over noble's aeskw, with the key-encryption key (16, 24 or 32 bytes, a key-type param) and the input as bytes. The IV is the RFC 3394 default, A6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6, fixed by noble, so CyberChef's IV parameter is not offered (a custom IV is not RFC 3394's algorithm as noble implements it). The input must be a multiple of 8 bytes and at least 16 (E_COERCE otherwise, as CyberChef). RFC 5649 padding is not offered, because CyberChef does not offer it. The output is raw bytes (chain hex:encode for CyberChef's Hex output). |
| AES Key Unwrap | redesigned | `aes-kw:unwrap` | The inverse of aes-kw:wrap under the same key-encryption key, with the same IV and no IV or padding parameters for the reason given for AES Key Wrap. The wrapped key must be a multiple of 8 bytes and at least 24 (E_COERCE otherwise). A wrong key or corrupted data fails the RFC 3394 integrity check: E_COERCE, and no key data is returned (CyberChef reports an IV mismatch error). |
| Pseudo-Random Number Generator | redesigned | `prng:bytes` | Bytes out: a number of random bytes (32 by default, 0 to 1 MiB) from the host CSPRNG (crypto.getRandomValues, never Math.random). CyberChef's Hex, Integer, Byte array and Raw output menu is a chain step (hex:encode, base64:encode, and so on). Like CyberChef the input is ignored. A host with no random source is E_PRIMITIVE. |
| Pseudo-Random Prime Generator | not yet |  |  |
| Enigma | covered | `enigma:encrypt` | Enigma I, M3 and M4 with the historical rotors, reflectors and plugboard; one reciprocal word (alias decrypt). |
| Bombe | redesigned | `bombe:search` | One Forge-native word covers both Bombe operations: give three rotors for a single rotor order. It searches all 17,576 start positions with a crib at an offset, using the menu, the diagonal board and the test register, and lists the stops with the steckers deduced and a decryption preview made with enigma:encrypt. Enigma I and M3 only (no M4); stops are window letters at the start of the message. |
| Multiple Bombe | redesigned | `bombe:search` | The same word: give more than three rotors (up to five, 60 orders) and every order of three of them is searched, left rotor first; the output names the rotor order of each stop. Capped by rotor orders times menu edges so that a run finishes inside a bake. |
| Typex | redesigned | `typex:encrypt` | Real Typex rotor wirings were never published, so there is no built-in rotor set: the five rotor wirings, reflector, notches and reversed rotors are parameters (validated permutations of A-Z), with clearly labelled non-historical example defaults. The conventions (rotors written left to right with the signal entering at the right, notch letters tested after the step, reversed rotors as neg o inverse o neg, the entry plugboard as a 26-letter wiring entering c as -P(c), Enigma-style stepping with the double step) follow CyberChef's for compatibility; the real Typex conventions are unpublished. |
| Lorenz | redesigned | `lorenz:encrypt`, `lorenz:decrypt` | Two words with one set of parameters (model SZ40, SZ42a or SZ42b, the P5 attachment, KH, ZMUG, BREAM or custom wheel patterns, twelve start positions, text or ITA2 in and out); decrypt exists because the P5 limitation makes the key depend on the plain text. |
| Colossus | redesigned | `colossus:count` | A counting run over the start positions of two chi wheels with a Boolean condition on delta Z and delta chi (the 1+2 break-in by default), a set total and a table of the best settings; it does not model the plug panels and the tape reader of the machine, and it does not search three wheels at once. |
| SIGABA | covered | `sigaba:crypt` | One word with a mode parameter (encrypt or decrypt), the rotor choice, orientation (R suffix) and start positions of the three banks, and optional rotor wirings; the default wirings are Forge's own, not the historical ones. The index rotor offset (+d for digit d) follows CyberChef's convention for compatibility; the sources do not fix it. |
| Flask Session Decode | redesigned | `flask-session:decode` | itsdangerous's URLSafeTimedSerializer as Flask uses it, in FL over base64. Decodes the payload.timestamp.signature cookie to the session JSON text as written (not parsed). The View TimeStamp option is the timestamp param (default false); with it the result is {"payload":...,"timestamp":N}. The timestamp is read as itsdangerous writes it, the shortest big-endian integer, where CyberChef reads exactly 4 bytes. A cookie whose payload Flask compressed with zlib (it starts with a dot) is E_COERCE with a message saying decompression comes with the compression vocabulary, because the runtime has no inflate yet (CyberChef cannot read these either). CyberChef cannot decode a cookie with non-ASCII text (it fails), which is read here as UTF-8. |
| Flask Session Sign | redesigned | `flask-session:sign` | Signs a session JSON as a Flask cookie: salt cookie-session by default, the 'hmac' key derivation HMAC(secret, salt), a SHA-1 (default) or SHA-256 signature over payload.timestamp, url-safe base64 without padding. The key and the salt are key params (CyberChef's toggle encodings, minus Decimal and Binary which are chain steps); an empty key is E_RANGE (Secret key required) and an empty salt means the default, as CyberChef. The input JSON text is used as given. The time is the clock (the +time effect) unless the added timestamp param pins it (Unix seconds above 0; 0 is now), which also makes the word reproducible. Never compresses. CyberChef signs the re-serialised JSON, written as Latin-1 (it keeps the low byte of each character, so non-ASCII text comes out wrong); here the text is signed as given in UTF-8. For ASCII compact JSON the cookie equals CyberChef's. |
| Flask Session Verify | redesigned | `flask-session:verify` | Checks the signature as flask-session:sign writes it (E_COERCE when it does not verify, as CyberChef's Invalid signature) and returns {"valid":true,"payload":...} with ,"timestamp":N when the timestamp param is set (default true), as text rather than a parsed object. Same key, salt and algorithm params as flask-session:sign. A compressed (leading dot) payload is E_COERCE until the compression vocabulary exists. The age of the cookie is not checked, as in CyberChef. |

## Hashing (48)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analyse hash | covered | `hash-analysis:analyse` | Takes hex text and returns a text report: length in hex characters, bytes and bits, and the hashing functions whose digest has that size (every size CyberChef names, down to the 4-bit checksums, so an odd number of hex digits is accepted). The table is Forge's own and lists some functions that Forge has not implemented. Text that is not hex is an error. |
| Generate all checksums | redesigned | `generate-all:checksums` | A text report, one checksum per line with its hex: the 171 CRC presets, Adler-32 and Fletcher-8, -16, -32 and -64, with the same Length and Include names parameters. The CRCs are computed by one private primitive (171 CRCs of 64 KiB in FL would be about 200 million steps) that the tests hold equal to crc:checksum; the order of the lines is the CRC table first, then the other checksums. |
| Generate all hashes | redesigned | `generate-all:hashes` | A text report, one hash per line with its hex, built from the digest words: MD2 to MD6, SHA-0 to SHA-3, Keccak, SHAKE, RIPEMD, HAS-160, Whirlpool, BLAKE2, BLAKE3, Streebog, GOST, Snefru, SM3, the LM hash, the NT hash and SSDEEP, with the same Length and Include names parameters. The LM hash line sits where CyberChef has it, just before the NT hash; like the NT hash it reads the input as UTF-8 text and shows a note on its line (the report still completes) for input that is not text it can take (the LM hash takes characters up to U+00FF only). Not included: Whirlpool-0 and Whirlpool-T, and the CTPH line (see CTPH). Lines CyberChef does not have: SHA-512/224 and /256, BLAKE3 and Snefru. |
| MD2 | covered | `md2:digest` | Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). Only the standard 18 rounds of RFC 1319 exist; CyberChef's Rounds parameter is not supported. |
| MD4 | covered | `md4:digest` | RFC 1320. Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| MD5 | covered | `md5:digest` | No parameters. Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| MD6 | covered | `md6:digest` | Parameters size (bits, a multiple of 8, 8 to 512, default 256), levels (L, 0 to 64, default 64) and key (up to 64 bytes), with CyberChef's defaults. Sizes that are not a multiple of 8 bits are not supported. The round count is the report's default (40 + size/4, at least 80 with a key). |
| SHA0 | covered | `sha0:digest` | FIPS 180 (1993). Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). Only the standard 80 rounds exist; a Rounds parameter is not supported. |
| SHA1 | covered | `sha1:digest` | No parameters. Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| SHA2 | covered | `sha2:digest` | One word with a size parameter: 224, 256, 384, 512 (the default, as in CyberChef), 512/224, 512/256. Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). CyberChef's Rounds parameter is not supported: only the FIPS 180-4 round counts exist. |
| SHA3 | covered | `sha3:digest` | One word with a size parameter in bits: 224, 256, 384, 512 (the default, as in CyberChef). Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| SM3 | covered | `sm3:digest` | Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). CyberChef's Length and Rounds parameters are not supported: the standard GB/T 32905-2016 has one 256-bit output and 64 rounds. |
| Keccak | covered | `keccak:digest` | One word with a size parameter in bits: 224, 256, 384, 512 (the default, as in CyberChef), with the original Keccak padding (not SHA-3). |
| Shake | redesigned | `shake:digest` | The output length is in bytes (1 to 65536, default 64), where CyberChef's Size is in bits (default 512, so the default is the same 64 bytes; the bits are a multiple of 8 in Forge). The variant is 128 or 256, the security strength in bits, as in CyberChef's Capacity (default 256 in both). |
| RIPEMD | covered | `ripemd:digest` | One word with a size choice of 128, 160, 256 or 320 (default 320, as in CyberChef). Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). ripemd160:digest also exists, for HMAC. |
| HAS-160 | covered | `has160:digest` | Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). CyberChef's Rounds parameter is not supported: only the standard 80 steps exist. |
| Whirlpool | covered | `whirlpool:digest` | The final ISO/IEC 10118-3 version, raw bytes (chain hex:encode). The Whirlpool-0 and Whirlpool-T variants and the Rounds parameter are not offered: the variants have no citable vectors in the original papers, and Whirlpool-0 has a different, random S-box. Only the standard 10 rounds exist. |
| Snefru | covered | `snefru:digest` | Size 128 or 256 (default 128) and Rounds 2, 4 or 8 (default 8), as in CyberChef; CyberChef also accepts other sizes in steps of 32 bits up to 480, which the Snefru reference does not define. Raw bytes (chain hex:encode). Implemented from Merkle's Xerox reference distribution 2.5a, whose S-boxes it uses. |
| BLAKE2b | redesigned | `blake2b:digest` | The output size is in bytes (16, 20, 32, 48 or 64, default 64), where CyberChef's Size is in bits (128, 160, 256, 384, 512, default 512). The key is an optional key of up to 64 bytes in any of the key encodings. |
| BLAKE2s | redesigned | `blake2s:digest` | The output size is in bytes (16, 20 or 32, default 32), where CyberChef's Size is in bits (128, 160, 256, default 256). The key is an optional key of up to 32 bytes in any of the key encodings. |
| BLAKE3 | covered | `blake3:digest` | The output length is in bytes (1 to 65536, default 32, the BLAKE3 specification's default output; CyberChef's default is 16). The key is an optional 32-byte key, as in CyberChef. |
| Ascon Hash | covered | `ascon:hash` | Ascon-Hash256 of NIST SP 800-232, the only variant CyberChef offers. The output is the 32 raw bytes (chain hex:encode for CyberChef's hex text). |
| Ascon MAC | redesigned | `ascon:mac` | Ascon-Mac with a 16-byte key param (E_RANGE otherwise) and a 16-byte tag, as CyberChef. It is the PRF-based MAC of the Ascon designers' reference code (ascon-c, the asconmacv13 known answers), which CyberChef labels with SP 800-232 although that standard does not define a MAC. The output is raw bytes (chain hex:encode for hex text). |
| GOST Hash | covered | `gost:digest`, `streebog:digest` | GOST R 34.11-94 is gost:digest with an sbox parameter: test (RFC 5831, CyberChef's D-TEST) or cryptopro (RFC 4357, CyberChef's D-A, the default here and the one its Generate all hashes uses). CyberChef's own default, E-TEST, and its other E-* sets are the sets of the 28147-89 cipher, not hash parameter sets, and are not offered. GOST R 34.11-2012 is the separate streebog:digest. Only the test and CryptoPro hash S-box sets are offered. Raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| Streebog | covered | `streebog:digest` | Size 256 or 512, as in CyberChef. Raw bytes (chain hex:encode), in the byte order of the RFC 6986 examples reversed (little-endian), which is the conventional digest string. |
| SSDEEP | covered | `ssdeep:digest` | Context triggered piecewise hashing (Kornblum 2006) as the reference ssdeep program computes it. The result is text, blocksize:hash1:hash2, not bytes: it is a structured string that the compare word reads piece by piece. |
| CTPH | redesigned | `ssdeep:ctph` | CyberChef's CTPH is a second implementation of the same idea whose text differs from its own SSDEEP (the block size is written in another form and the pieces differ), and its algorithm is not documented beyond that library. Forge has one fuzzy hash, the reference ssdeep one, and ctph is an alias of ssdeep:digest under the name of the 2006 paper; the text is not CyberChef's CTPH text. |
| Compare SSDEEP hashes | covered | `ssdeep:compare` | The 0 to 100 score of the reference algorithm: block size check, runs of more than three equal characters cut to three, a common substring of 7 characters, a weighted edit distance (insert and remove 1, replace 2) and the cap for small block sizes. The first hash is the data input and the second is the other parameter. Text that is not an ssdeep hash is an error here, where CyberChef scores it 0. |
| Compare CTPH hashes | redesigned | `ssdeep:compare-ctph` | CyberChef's Compare CTPH hashes reads its own CTPH text, which Forge does not produce (see CTPH). compare-ctph is an alias of ssdeep:compare and scores ssdeep text. |
| HMAC | covered | `hmac:digest` | Hash choice: md2, md4, md5, sha0, sha1, sha224, sha256 (the default; CyberChef's first choice, and so its default, is MD2), sha384, sha512, sha512/224, sha512/256, ripemd128, ripemd160, ripemd256, ripemd320, has160, whirlpool and snefru, which are every CyberChef choice except Whirlpool-0 and Whirlpool-T (Forge does not implement those variants of Whirlpool). The four SHA-3 sizes (sha3-224, sha3-256, sha3-384, sha3-512) are extra: CyberChef's HMAC has no SHA-3. snefru is Snefru with a 128-bit output and 8 passes, as CyberChef uses. The key is a key param in any of the key encodings (utf8, hex, latin1 or base64; CyberChef also offers Decimal, which Forge does not), empty by default. The output is the raw MAC bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. Blake2 and BLAKE3 keyed modes are their own words. |
| CMAC | redesigned | `cmac:digest` | NIST SP 800-38B and RFC 4493. The input is the message, the key is a key param (hex, utf8, latin1 or base64) and the algorithm is AES (default) or TDES (CyberChef's Triple DES). AES takes 16, 24 or 32 bytes, Triple DES 16 (two-key, K3 = K1) or 24 bytes, and another length is E_RANGE. The output is the raw tag, 16 bytes for AES and 8 for Triple DES (chain hex:encode for CyberChef's hex text). The block cipher is a private primitive that calls the TypeScript AES and Triple DES block functions directly, because the block words of those vocabularies are private. |
| Bcrypt compare | redesigned | `bcrypt:compare` | The input is the password and the hash is a str param. The result is a bool, where CyberChef returns the text Match: <password> or No match. A string that is not a well-formed bcrypt hash (2a, 2b or 2y, a cost of 04 to 31, 22 salt and 31 hash characters) is E_COERCE, where CyberChef raises an error; a cost in it above 16 is E_RANGE. The comparison is constant time. |
| Bcrypt parse | covered | `bcrypt:parse` | The input is the hash text. The report has CyberChef's four lines: Rounds, Salt (prefix, cost and the 22 salt characters), Password hash and Full hash. A string that is not a well-formed bcrypt hash is E_COERCE. Parsing does no hashing, so any cost from 04 to 31 is reported. |
| Argon2 | redesigned | `argon2:derive` | The input is the password. Salt (default the text somesalt), iterations (3), memory in KiB (4096), parallelism (1), hash length in bytes (32) and type (argon2i, argon2d or argon2id; default argon2i) are CyberChef's. The output is a choice of encoded (the PHC string $argon2i$v=19$m=4096,t=3,p=1$salt$hash, as ASCII bytes; the default, as CyberChef) or raw hash bytes; CyberChef's Hex hash is raw chained through hex:encode. The salt must be at least 8 bytes. Limits (E_RANGE): memory 8 to 262,144 KiB (256 MiB), iterations 1 to 64, memory times iterations at most 1,048,576 (about 2.5 s), parallelism 1 to 64, length 4 to 1024; the defaults take about 40 ms. |
| Argon2 compare | redesigned | `argon2:compare` | The input is the password and the encoded hash is a str param. The result is a bool, where CyberChef returns the text Match: <password> or No match. A string that is not a well-formed encoded Argon2 hash (type, optional version, m, t and p, unpadded base64 salt of at least 8 bytes and hash of at least 4) is E_COERCE, where CyberChef reports No match; the cost in the string is held to the limits of argon2:derive (E_RANGE). The comparison is constant time. |
| NT Hash | covered | `nthash:digest` | MD4 of the UTF-16LE text (MS-NLMP NTOWFv1), 16 raw bytes. Takes text, not bytes. |
| LM Hash | redesigned | `lmhash:digest` | The password is the input text, upper-cased and then cut at 14 bytes, as CyberChef does (so a character that upper-cases to two, such as the German sharp s, counts twice). It is encoded as ISO 8859-1 where CyberChef's library writes the low byte of each character. The output is the 16 raw bytes (chain hex:encode for CyberChef's hex text). A character above U+00FF cannot be written in ISO 8859-1 and is E_COERCE, where CyberChef's library keeps its low byte. |
| MurmurHash3 | covered | `murmur3:digest` | MurmurHash3 x86_32 with a 32-bit seed (default 0), written in FL; CyberChef offers only this 32-bit variant too, and the x86_128 and x64_128 variants are not implemented here either. Returns the 32-bit value as 4 raw bytes in big-endian order, the usual hex form (chain hex:encode); CyberChef shows the same value as an unsigned decimal (or signed, with its option). Forge hashes the bytes of the input; CyberChef hashes the low 8 bits of each character, so the two agree for byte-valued text and differ for text beyond Latin-1. |
| Fletcher-8 Checksum | covered | `fletcher:checksum` | size 8. The output is 1 raw byte (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Fletcher-16 Checksum | covered | `fletcher:checksum` | size 16. The output is 2 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Fletcher-32 Checksum | covered | `fletcher:checksum` | size 32. The output is 4 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Fletcher-64 Checksum | covered | `fletcher:checksum` | size 64. The output is 8 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Adler-32 Checksum | covered | `adler32:checksum` | The output is 4 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Luhn Checksum | redesigned | `luhn:check-digit`, `luhn:validate` | Two words, the check digit and a validity flag, instead of a three-line report whose "validated string" is not a validation. The radix is a parameter in both (an even number from 2 to 36, default 10). CyberChef's "Checksum" line, the sum modulo the radix of the input as given, is not offered on its own: validate is true when that sum is 0. The check digit is one lowercase character, as in CyberChef. The empty input gives the empty check digit in both; validate is false for it. |
| CRC Checksum | covered | `crc:checksum`, `crc:custom` | Presets by CyberChef's names (all 171, with the same parameters); custom parameters in crc:custom. The output is raw bytes (ceil(width/8) of them), not hex text padded to ceil(width/4) digits. The default is the CRC-32 preset (CyberChef's default is Custom, with width 0), and crc:custom defaults to the CRC-32 parameters (CyberChef's are all 0) and accepts widths of 1 to 82 bits. |
| TCP/IP Checksum | covered | `tcpip:checksum` | Folds the carry until it is gone (RFC 1071), while CyberChef folds it once, so for some inputs (for example the bytes ff ff ff ff 00 01) CyberChef prints "-1" where RFC 1071 gives fffe. The output is 2 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), always four hex digits; CyberChef shows hex text without padding to four digits (0x0f67 shows as "f67"). Confirmed in CyberChef's TCPIPChecksum.mjs: one fold, then Utils.hex(0xffff - csum) with the default padding of 2. |
| XOR Checksum | covered | `xor-checksum:checksum` | The default blocksize is 4, the same as CyberChef's. The output is blocksize raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. A short last block is treated as zero-padded in both. The blocksize is 1 to 65536 in Forge; CyberChef accepts any positive integer. |
| Parity Bit | covered | `parity:encode`, `parity:decode` | Two words, encode and decode, instead of an Encode/Decode switch. parity:decode verifies the parity by default (verify=true) and raises E_COERCE on a mismatch or an unexpected character, whereas CyberChef's decode strips the bit without checking; verify=false gives CyberChef's behaviour. The one exception is an empty block between delimiters, for which decode raises E_COERCE ("no parity bit to remove") even with verify=false, where CyberChef returns the empty block. The default position is end, where CyberChef's first (default) Position is Start; the default mode is even in both. Encoding is the same. |

## Flow control (10)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Magic | not yet |  |  |
| Fork | redesigned | `step:fork` | A structural fork step (RECIPES section 3.2) holds its child steps; split and join are part of the step. |
| Subsection | redesigned | `step:subsection` | A structural step that runs its children on each regex match and leaves the rest of the data alone. |
| Merge | redesigned | `step:fork` | No separate step: a fork step joins its pieces when its children end. |
| Register | not yet |  |  |
| Label | redesigned | `step:repeat` | Loops are structural repeat steps (a count or until stable), not labels. |
| Jump | redesigned | `step:repeat` | Loops are structural repeat steps (a count or until stable), not jumps. |
| Conditional Jump | redesigned | `step:if` | Branching is a tree: an if step holds then and else steps, so there are no labels or jumps. |
| Return | not yet |  |  |
| Comment | redesigned | `step:comment` | A structural comment step with no effect on the data. |
